title: Continuity at a Point (Formal Definition)
notes: **Formal definition:** A function f(x) is continuous at x = a if three conditions are satisfied.
**Condition 1:** f(a) is defined (the function exists at x = a).
**Condition 2:** lim(x→a) f(x) exists (both left and right limits exist and are equal).
**Condition 3:** lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a) (the limit equals the function value).
**All three conditions must be met** for continuity at a point — failure of any one means discontinuity.
**Continuity on an interval:** f is continuous on [a,b] if it's continuous at every point in the interval.
**Algebraic continuity:** Polynomials, rational functions (where defined), trig functions, exponential functions are continuous on their domains.
**Breaking continuity:** Discontinuities occur when any of the three conditions fail.
confusion: Continuity at a point requires all THREE conditions — missing even one means the function is discontinuous there.
f(a) existing is necessary but not sufficient — the limit must also exist and equal f(a).
Don't confuse continuity with differentiability — all differentiable functions are continuous, but not vice versa.
A function can be continuous on an interval but discontinuous at the endpoints if defined appropriately.
The formal definition uses limits, connecting continuity directly to the limit concept.
practice: Show that f(x) = x² + 2x - 1 is continuous at x = 3 by verifying all three conditions.
For f(x) = {x+1 if x≠2, 5 if x=2}, check continuity at x = 2. Which condition fails?
Determine if g(x) = 1/(x-1) is continuous at x = 1. Explain which condition(s) fail.
Prove that h(x) = √x is continuous at x = 4 using the formal definition.
Find the value of k that makes f(x) = {x²+k if x≤2, 3x-1 if x>2} continuous at x = 2.
universalFacts: The formal definition of continuity was refined by Cauchy in the 19th century.
Continuous functions preserve limits: if xₙ → a, then f(xₙ) → f(a).
The composition of continuous functions is continuous — a fundamental property.
Continuous functions on closed intervals have the intermediate value property.
Most elementary functions encountered in calculus are continuous on their domains.
